newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE - Bangladesh's BRAC brings hopes, smiles.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bangladesh's BRAC brings hopes, smiles.

text.p: Zahera Begum used to sleep in a virtually roofless home with her six malnourished children, but today she is a proud mother with a thriving business.
"My nightmares are over and my dreams coming true," said the 55-year-old woman, still haunted by her dreadful past.
"My husband was the only earning member in the family but it was not enough to ensure two square meals a day," she told Reuters at her Manikganj village 60 km (40 miles) north of Dhaka.
Begum now owns a small plot of farmland, three tin-roofed houses, a poultry firm and cows.
"My monthly net income is 2,000 taka ($46.50). My grandchildren are attending school. I have learned how to read and write," she said.

And all this was made possible through funding and counselling by the Bangladesh Rural Advancement Committee (BRAC), a micro-credit organisation that has revolutionised the lives of the rural poor, especially women, in Bangladesh.
RELENTLESS BATTLE AGAINST POVERTY

Begum, like many other women in this south Asian country, launched a relentless battle against grinding poverty with a credit from the BRAC. She borrowed 5,000 taka ($116) in 1987 and now has net assets of 10 times that.
"BRAC not only provides credit, they also facilitate the marketing of my poultry products, offer advice and teach borrowers how to read and write," Begum said.
"Now I have gained some social status. The villagers come to me to take my advice and I feel honoured."
Rahima Khatun, 32, took a loan of 8,000 taka ($186) from the BRAC, a non-government organisation (NGO), four years ago to try to save her impoverished family from starving.
Now Khatun has a small home, wears gold ornaments and smiles as she tends her poultry.
"Since I got married six years ago I faced all sorts of problems, including an attack of tuberculosis. I thought I would die," she told Reuters.
"Luckily I got in touch with BRAC and the health service and it helped me overcome the disease. I am now fully cured."
BRAC MADE ALL THE DIFFERENCE
Since its debut in 1972, the BRAC has built up a strong fight against malnutrition, illiteracy, disease, population growth and unemployment in the villages of Bangladesh.

At first its activities were confined to the resettlement of refugees after the 1971 war that led to the birth of Bangladesh. By 1976, BRAC had started to focus exclusively on the poorest of the poor -- the landless, marginal farmers, village artisans and women vulnerable social and economic injustice.

The United Nations sponsored Human Development Report (HDR) 1997 said: "By 1995, BRAC had emerged as one of the largest NGOs in the world, covering sixty out of sixty-four districts of Bangladesh, with a total membership of 1.5 million, 85 percent of them women."

The report said Bangladesh had a strong tradition of NGO movements -- it is estimated that NGOs currently cover about 78 percent of the villages in Bangladesh and about 24 million of the country's 120 million people benefit from their activities.
"About $500 million worth of projects are approved annually by donors for implementation by NGOs in Bangladesh," the report added.
Besides BRAC, Bangladesh's other major NGO is the Grameen Bank, founded by Dr. Mohammad Yunus, a front-runner in the micro-credit movement.
BRAC ENCOURAGES CLIENTS TO HELP THEMSELVES

BRAC has set up two organisations in every village where it operates -- one for men and one for women. Only the landless, or those owning less than half an acre (2,000 square metres) of land, are eligible for membership.
"Members are encouraged to join hands to find solutions to their problems. Small credits are given without any collateral," said Fazle Hasan Abed, BRAC's founder and executive director.
BRAC operates a range of income-generating activities and has 18,000 staff and more than 33,000 part-time teachers in villages. By the beginning of 1997, there were 1.8 million members (clients).

Abed said the BRAC clients had so far collectively saved more than one billion taka ($30 million). And in 1996 alone, they borrowed more than five billion taka ($128 million) for productive enterprises, repaying virtually all of it on time.

A million women were actively involved in poultry projects, Abed said. And 25 million mulberry trees had been planted to support silkworm enterprises that produced 43.5 tonnes of silk between 1992 and 1995, half the entire national production.
The U.N. report said: "One of the outstanding successes of BRAC is a non-formal education programme which was started in 1984."

BRAC runs two types of schools -- one for 8 to 10-year-old children and the other for those 11-14 years. There is one teacher for every 30 students. More than 72 percent of the students are girls, while 95 percent of the teachers are women.
BRAC has established 35,000 schools that accommodate 1.2 million students. Tuition and accessories like books and pencils are given free.

It also undertakes health care. The report said: "Its (BRAC's) Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) programme is implementing a nation-wide battle against diarrhoea...99 percent of mothers in Bangladesh have been given training by BRAC workers, enabling them to treat at home."
FOCUS IS ON WOMEN AND SOCIAL CHANGES
"BRAC's current focus is on sustainable development and empowerment of the poor...(and) we consider women as a key engine of change within the family and community," Abed said.
By the turn of the century, BRAC plans to bring three million families within its folds.

The rate of credit recovery under BRAC programmes was 98 percent. "The rate of two percent loss is genuine," Abed said. "They cannot pay due to crop damage, natural disasters and other unavoidable reasons."
